You are COVID Trials AI, a research assistant that answers questions about COVID-19 from a database of 10,269 ClinicalTrials.gov study records (1,096 with posted results) and 1,630 open-access papers that report those trials. People asking range from researchers and clinicians to members of the public.

How to answer:
- Base factual claims on what your tools return, and cite each one right after the claim with its ID in square brackets, like [NCT04381936] or [PMC9006771]. Cite only sources you retrieved in this conversation. If the database lacks good evidence, say so plainly instead of filling gaps from memory; brief general background is fine if you label it as such.
- Weigh the evidence. Large randomized controlled trials outweigh small, open-label or observational studies. Say what kind of study each finding comes from (design and size), and point out when studies disagree and why that might be.
- For exact numbers prefer posted registry results (get_trial); use papers for context and interpretation.
- When a question calls for statistics (pooling trials, risk ratios, rates, confidence intervals), compute them with code execution using numbers you retrieved. Run every calculation as code, even simple ones, rather than working it out in your head. Show the input numbers in a table, name the method and its assumptions, and say when trials are too different to combine. Watch for arms of the same trial that share a placebo group: pooling them counts those placebo patients twice.
- Write for the person asking: start with a short bottom line in plain language, then the details. Briefly define technical terms.
- This is research information, not medical advice. When a question is about someone's own care, say once, briefly, that decisions should be made with a clinician.
- Coverage: studies registered with COVID-19 as a condition, collected November 2026. Only papers linked from the registry are included, so some published trials are missing. Mention this when it limits an answer.

Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID in Adolescents (NCT06147050)
Official title: Pilot Study of an Adaptive, Double-blind, Randomized, Placebo-controlled Study to Evaluate the Effect of Metformin in Reducing Fatigue in Long COVID Adolescent Patients With Chronic Fatigue Syndrome
Type: INTERVENTIONAL; phase: PHASE3; allocation: RANDOMIZED; masking: TRIPLE
Status: UNKNOWN; start: 2024-04; enrollment: 16
Sponsor: Purpose Life Sciences
Conditions: Long COVID
Interventions: DRUG: Metformin; OTHER: Placebo
Primary outcomes: Mean Pediatric Quality of Life Multidimensional Fatigue Scale (PedsQL-MFS) score at 90 days post-randomization
Summary: Long Covid is a multisystem condition comprising often severe symptoms that follow a severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection. Long COVID often manifests as fatigue and neurocognitive impairment (also referred to as 'brain fog'). Based on two systematic reviews of Covid-19 cases in neonates, children and adolescents under 19 years of age, fatigue caused by Long Covid can persist for years and can lead to work disability and labour shortages, posing a public health emergency with lasting health, mental, and economic impacts. To date, no treatment has shown to be broadly effective for the treatment of Long Covid. An experimental study has demonstrated that metformin, a common diabetes drug, might reduce the incidence of long COVID if given during the acute phase of COVID-19. The study, however, did not look at whether metformin would be effective as a treatment for those who already have long COVID. It also did not report the results by age groups, so it is not clear if the effect of metformin differs for people younger than 35 years of age. Therefore, a pilot, adaptive randomized controlled trial, which will evaluate the feasibility of conducting a large platform trial and will also evaluate the efficacy and safety of using metformin (versus placebo, a look-alike substance with no active ingredient) in managing fatigue in long COVID adolescent patients with persistent (long term) features of fatigue (chronic fatigue syndrome) has been proposed.

[PMC8351223] Inflammasome activation at the crux of severe COVID-19 (2021) | section: Clinical interventions | trials: NCT05226754 | license: unspecified
Multiple phase II clinical trials are testing direct NLRP3 inhibition in patients with either mild or severe COVID-19 (Novartis, NCT04382053; Olatec Therapeutics, NCT04540120) (Table 1). In animal models, NLRP3 inhibition reduces cytokine release and lung inflammation in influenza A virus infection159, and the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 reduced caspase 1 activation and secretion of IL-1β in primary human monocytes infected with SARS-CoV-2 in vitro52. Another inhibitor of NLRP3, the sulfonylurea diabetes drug glyburide, reduced IL-6 secretion by SARS-CoV-2-infected human monocytes65. These data suggest that NLRP3 inhibition may be a superior strategy against COVID-19 in comparison with IL-1 inhibition. Indirect NLRP3 inhibition is also being tested by administration of the microtubule-depolymerizing drug colchicine, which among its other effects is a well-tolerated inhibitor of inflammasome formation160,161. A small randomized controlled trial in patients with moderate to severe disease demonstrated its ability to reduce oxygen requirement and hospitalization; in this study, low overall mortality precluded a determination of its effect on death162. Another study showed that patients with COVID-19 treated with colchicine had a significantly decreased rate of hospitalization or death combined, although neither the rate of hospitalization nor the rate of death was significantly reduced on its own and the study has not yet been peer reviewed163. The diabetes drug metformin indirectly inhibits NLRP3 by regulating mTOR, and its use is significantly associated with reduced mortality among patients with COVID-19 and type 2 diabetes. Metformin was also recently shown to inhibit NLRP3 activation and lung inflammation in SARS-CoV-2-infected mice164,165.

[PMC9006771] Effect of Early Treatment with Ivermectin among Patients with Covid-19 (2022) | section: Methods > Trial Design and Oversight | trials: NCT04727424 | license: unspecified
We conducted this randomized, adaptive platform trial for the investigation of the efficacy of repurposed treatments for Covid-19 among adult outpatients at high risk for hospitalization.10 The trial was designed and conducted in partnership with local public health authorities from 12 cities in Brazil in order to simultaneously test potential treatments for early Covid-19 with the use of a master protocol. A master protocol defines prospective decision criteria for discontinuing interventions for futility, stopping owing to superiority of an intervention over placebo, or adding new interventions. Interventions that have been evaluated in this trial thus far include hydroxychloroquine and lopinavir–ritonavir (both in protocol 1)11 and metformin, ivermectin administered for 1 day, ivermectin administered for 3 days, doxazosin, pegylated interferon lambda, and fluvoxamine (all in protocol 2), as compared with matching placebos. The full trial protocol with the statistical analysis plan has been published previously10 and is available with the full text of this article at NEJM.org.

[PMC7347402] Fasting blood glucose at admission is an independent predictor for 28-day mortality in patients with COVID-19 without previous diagnosis of diabetes: a multi-centre retrospective study (2020) | section: Discussion | trials: NCT04970719 | license: unspecified
Although insulin treatment for critically ill patients has become a standard of care, efficacy might well vary with different ICUs. A study published in 2001 reported that intensive insulin therapy with blood glucose maintained at or below 6 mmol/l reduced morbidity and mortality in critically ill patients in surgical ICUs [32]. However, subsequent studies on intensive insulin therapy of critically ill patients in medical ICUs showed that this treatment could reduce morbidity but not mortality [33]. The debate over this issue remains, and a study published in 2009 found that intensive glycaemic control could increase mortality in adults in ICUs, but increasing target glucose levels to 10 mmol/l could reduce mortality [34]. A recent review separately examined surgical and medical patients and suggested that, to treat hyperglycaemia, insulin therapy should be used to maintain the glucose level between 8 mmol/l and 10 mmol/l. This treatment could reduce the mortality and morbidity resulting from high FBG and lower the occasional risk of hypoglycaemia associated with intensive insulin therapy [35].

This study has several limitations. First, this was a retrospective study. Second, we did not cover HbA1c, a long-term glycaemic control indicator that helps distinguish patients with poor long-term glycaemic control from those with stress hyperglycaemia. Finally, because our results were premised only on the glucose levels at admission, we might have underestimated the risks associated with hyperglycaemia (assuming that patients with the highest glucose levels are more likely to be treated in the hospital), and we did not have sufficient data to study the effect of glucose-lowering treatment (e.g. insulin, metformin) on the outcome of our patients. However, we believe that acute hyperglycaemia is more important than long-term glycaemic control in predicting the prognosis of hospitalised COVID-19 patients.

---

[PMC10103649] A review of cytokine-based pathophysiology of Long COVID symptoms (2023) | section: Therapeutic implications > Long COVID | trials: NCT06294756 | license: CC BY
Ultimately, the prevention of Long COVID is an equally important topic to be addressed. The effect of vaccinations in decreasing Long COVID has been discussed above. Modulating and decreasing the initial immune inflammatory response in COVID-19 may be beneficial in reducing the incidence of Long COVID. A recent preprint indicated a 42% relative decrease (6.3% vs. 10.6%) in the incidence of Long COVID in participants who received early outpatient COVID-19 treatment with the drug metformin with known anti-inflammatory effects (290) compared to a matched placebo control group (291).

**Bottom line:** Yes. Metformin has been tested in several COVID-19 trials, mostly in outpatients with mild-to-moderate illness. The largest and best-designed trials found no clear benefit in preventing hospitalization or death. A few small trials were also run, and some were withdrawn.

**Main trials (randomized, placebo-controlled)**

- **COVID-OUT (NCT04510194)**, a 2×3 factorial trial of 1,323 non-hospitalized adults, tested metformin, ivermectin, and fluvoxamine against placebo.
  - Primary outcome (clinical progression within 14 days, meaning an ED visit, hospitalization, death, or low oxygen saturation): 154/652 on metformin vs 179/653 on placebo. That is a risk ratio of 0.86 (95% CI 0.72–1.04), which is not statistically significant [NCT04510194].
  - A secondary outcome, ED visit, hospitalization, or death, was lower on metformin: 27/652 vs 48/653 (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.36–0.89). This was not the primary endpoint, so treat it as a hypothesis-generating signal [NCT04510194].
  - Hospitalization or death by day 28 was 8/596 vs 19/601 [NCT04510194].
- **ACTIV-6 Arm G (NCT06042855)**, a large, double-blind outpatient trial with 3,214 participants (1,443 metformin, 1,548 placebo; 1000 mg/day for 14 days).
  - Hospitalization or death by day 28: 4 vs 3 events (HR 1.43, 95% CI 0.32–6.38). This is far too few events to say much [NCT06042855].
  - Median time to sustained recovery was 9 vs 10 days (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.89–1.03) [NCT06042855].
  - Time unwell over 14 days was essentially identical (11.55 vs 11.51 days) [NCT06042855].
- The Brazilian TOGETHER platform trial also tested metformin against placebo in outpatients at high risk [PMC9006771]. I did not retrieve its metformin-specific results, so I can't report them here.

**Smaller or incomplete studies**

- **NCT04625985** (Mexico): a randomized, double-blind trial of metformin glycinate in hospitalized patients. It enrolled only 20 participants, and no results are posted [NCT04625985].
- **NCT04626089**: a metformin glycinate trial in hospitalized patients with diabetes or metabolic syndrome. It was withdrawn before enrolling anyone [NCT04626089].
- **NCT04604678**: a metformin plus low-dose naltrexone pilot. It was withdrawn with zero enrollment [NCT04604678].
- **NCT06147050**: metformin for fatigue in adolescents with long COVID. This is a 16-person pilot with no results yet [NCT06147050].

**Interpretation**

- The largest trials (ACTIV-6, COVID-OUT) are the most reliable evidence. Neither showed a statistically significant benefit on its primary endpoint.
- COVID-OUT's secondary result looks favorable, but the primary endpoint was not significant. Given how many outcomes were tested, this should be read cautiously.
- Observational studies have linked metformin use to lower COVID mortality in people with diabetes. Those studies are confounded and aren't covered by the trial evidence above.
- This database covers only trials registered with COVID-19 as a condition and papers linked from the registry, so some published trials may be missing.

This is research information rather than medical advice. If you are considering metformin for your own COVID-19 or long COVID, please discuss it with a clinician, especially since it is already prescribed for diabetes.
